national.title: Why are investors freaking out even as the U.S. economy surges?
national.summary: The economy is sending mixed signals, with growth jumping while stocks gyrate. Here's what economists say is going on.
national.body: The U.S. economy is racing ahead, with new data showing that the country's gross domestic product rose at a blistering 4.3% pace in the third quarter. So why are investors hitting the panic button, causing stocks to swing wildly and bruising your 401(k) plan?The answer boils down to the relationship among inflation, interest rates and the Federal Reserve, along with mounting concerns on Wall Street that the artificial intelligence boom could turn to bust.Stocks on Wednesday show just how brittle investor sentiment is at the moment. Leading indexes plunged more than 1,000 points in morning activity, only to claw back much of those losses in afternoon trading. Where stocks go next, nobody knows.The S&P 500 index is now about 8% lower than its most recent high on Oct. 6, putting it close to a correction, or a decline of more than 10% from its recent peak. Also on Wednesday, the Bureau of Economic Analysis sharply raised its estimate for third-quarter growth from its previous forecast of 3.4%. That growth is being fueled by steady consumer spending and surging business investment, with large tech firms splurging on building out data centers and other infrastructure required to power AI.Americans benefit when the economy is growing, fueling consumer spending and hiring. But heady growth can also have a downside — especially when, as in the current moment, inflation is already running hot."In the simplest possible words, the economy is overheated, with demand exceeding supply. The consequence is a blowout of the trade deficit and inflation," HFE chief economist Carl B. Weinberg said in a research note.The link between AI and inflationAlthough inflation earlier in the year was largely driven by rising energy costs, more recent signals suggest that strong economic growth, fueled by heavy AI spending, is now the main factor driving up prices. Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee said last week that trillions in spending on data centers are contributing to the nation's "borderline disturbingly high" inflation.Newly released inflation data showed consumer prices rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September.Meanwhile, the admixture of high inflation and heady economic growth virtually cements a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike at its December meeting, and possibly additional hikes in early 2027, according to economists.Rate

national.title: Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast
national.summary: Divers found the bodies of three adult, one teenager aged 16, and two boys, aged 12 and 10, in the wreckage.
national.body:
Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says.

The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.

Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.

On Wednesday, the Jackson County Coroner's Office identified the passengers as Brent Stokes, 50, Michael Knox, 43, Arlyn Knox, 43, Hunter Stokes,16, Charles Holden Knox, 12 and Truett Knox, 10, according the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

The Coast Guard had previously said the young boys were 10 and eight years old.

Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

The Federal Aviation Administration said the plane was descending at 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute when contact was lost, according to a CBS affiliate in Biloxi, Mississippi.

national.title: Vance says Nvidia's Huang isn't under investigation; doesn't need a pardon
national.summary: Vice President JD Vance said he was assured Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang isn't under federal investigation.
national.body: Washington — Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday said he doesn't think Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang needs a presidential pardon, as he said the Justice Department and national security officials informed him that Huang isn't under federal investigation.Speaking to reporters after serving Thanksgiving dinner at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base near Dayton, Ohio, the vice president was asked about his involvement in Huang's reinstatement and the assurances he received that Huang isn't a national security risk. CBS News has reported that President Trump and Vance spoke repeatedly with Huang, Nvidia board members and their legal counsel."Well, number one, we were told that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters Wednesday. "And frankly, I think we have to, in our country, remember that we don't try people in the court of public opinion. ... But most importantly, at just I think a personal level, we received the assurances that he was not under any significant — he was under no investigation, and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence."Asked who gave him those assurances, Vance said he spoke with "multiple people in the United States government," including Attorney General Todd Blanche. Asked if he thinks Huang needs a pardon, the vice president said he doesn't. In an interview with the New York Post, the president said a pardon is "always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." But Vance told reporters, "I don't think he needs a pardon at all.""I haven't seen any evidence, again, that he committed a crime," Vance continued. "And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him. And again, I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation."Vance said "ultimately, it was the board's decision to bring Jensen Huang back." Nvidia's board reinstated Huang after President Trump urged them to do so. The president himself said he "convinced" the board to reinstate the ousted CEO. Mr. Trump owned millions of dollars in Nvidia stock as he pushed for Huang's reinstatement amid tanking stock prices.

national.title: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
national.summary: Despite widespread concern from residents ahead of the blast, officials say that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
national.body:
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked widespread fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".

President Donald Trump said reports showed the mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".

Plans to detonate the lead azide, a highly volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused multiple times before Wednesday's detonation following public outcry and legal challenges.

Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.

"We are watching EPA's [Environmental Protection Agency] MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," he added.

The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.

national.title: Kilmar Ábrego García arrives in Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
national.summary: His deportation to and return from El Salvador became a flashpoint in the debate the US president's immigration agenda.
national.body:
Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to an El Salvador jail became a flashpoint in President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, has left the US for Spain.

He took a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday. His lawyer said the relocation was temporary while Ábrego García sought eventually to return to the US.

After the US government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to face human trafficking charges that were later dropped.

The Trump administration had continued its attempts to deport him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.

Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday.

"Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."

national.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
national.summary: Swiss officials said relations would be kept through North Korea's embassy in Bern, and its own embassy in Beijing.
national.body:
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close amid a row over sanctions.

It said the move was in response to Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp. State media described this as "a blatant hostile act".

That camp is at the centre of claims that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

North Korea's foreign ministry said "any act of violating the sovereign rights" of the country and the interests of its citizens "can never be welcomed".

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.

Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.

The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.

Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997.

national.summary: Iran's U.N. envoy claims the U.S. military used Palantir and Anthropic AI systems to select some 2,000 targets over just four days.
national.body: The Iranian Foreign Ministry has called out Republican Sen. John Cornyn for a post on X criticizing Iran's alleged pursuit of nuclear weapons, however, the quote cited by the senator was actually about North Korean nuclear ambitions. The Texas senator cited International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi raising concern "about a rapidly built extension at the Yongbyon gas centrifuge uranium enrichment plant." Cornyn wrote on X, "Doesn't sound like the Iranian regime is giving up on its nuclear weapons aspirations." Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei correctly pointed out Grossi was speaking about Yongbyon, North Korea, and nothing to do with Iran. Cornyn serves on the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, one of the governing body's most important posts. Cornyn is on his way out of the Senate. He was soundly defeated by Ken Paxton in the Republican primary this spring. Paxton would eventually lose earlier this month to Democrat James Talarico. The post on X remains live 24 hours after the senator shared it.

national.summary: The operation was carried out in cooperation with the Colombian navy and the U.S. Joint Interagency Task Force South.

national.title: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 76 held hostage for 17 hours
national.summary: One gunman was killed after what the country's president described as a robbery of a cash-laden armoured car gone wrong.
national.body:
Colombian security forces have freed around 76 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.

Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 local time (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella described as a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money.

They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.

With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, de la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, killing one gunman.

Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.

Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage-takers. Four have been arrested.

De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".

He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation personally. He could be seen flanked by the commanders of the operation with a handgun strapped to his belt, in footage released following its conclusion.

national.summary: Maps released by the Army Tuesday show a possible plume of toxic dust after its detonation of munitions in Iowa drifting southwest toward northeast Missouri between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Wednesday.
national.body: Maps released by the Army Tuesday show a possible plume of toxic dust after its detonation of munitions in Iowa drifting southwest toward northeast Missouri between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Wednesday. The Army detonated about 5 tons of degraded lead azide, in 68 barrels, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown at 9 a.m. Wednesday. Following the blast, Army officials said mitigation efforts successfully reduced the risk of lead particles spreading."I believe absolutely that we reduced, as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and the safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa," Army Maj. Gen. Eric P. Shirley, the commander of the operation, said at a news conference.The Environmental Protection Agency reported that zero lead was detected in the air by four monitors stations in the area 15 minutes after the detonation. Those sensors continued to show the same readings two hours later, according to the EPA. Testing of levels in the region will continue, officials said.An earlier alert said some people within 5 miles southwest of the plant may be evacuated and told people up to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed. The Army moved the detonation from Friday, citing more favorable wind and time to add safety measures, according to a government court filing. A federal appeals court cleared the way Monday for the detonation after it had been delayed several times amid lawsuits from environmental groups and concerns from elected officials in Illinois and Iowa.The maps from Tuesday show the modeled dust plume from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m. Wednesday. By 9:45 a.m., the shaded area becomes a long oval running from near Burlington southwest toward the Missouri line.By early afternoon, the shaded area stretches far into northeast Missouri, passing Knox City. national.title: State Department reports downplay violence and corruption in countries that asylum seekers are fleeing
national.summary: The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and in some cases facts that don't stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are in fact often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.
national.body:
Tim Sullivan, Associated Press Tim Sullivan, Associated Press

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — In its travel advisories, the U.S. State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras' Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.

But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. "Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department," says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.

WATCH: Thousands of immigrants with legal status lose Medicaid coverage

The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94% during President Donald Trump's second term.

The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and in some cases facts that don't stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are in fact often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.

They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.

The reports have been "reverse-engineered," said Elliot Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analyzed the documents for the college's Migration and Asylum Lab.

national.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
national.summary: All three main US indexes were down in early trading, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq down almost 4%.
national.body:
Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down. The tech-dominated Nasdaq has shed over 2%.

The declines come amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment which has rattled investors in recent weeks.

Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta were also down.

Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased.

The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang after revelations of his extra marital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.

Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.

The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

national.title: Titanic postcard sent days before doomed voyage sells for pricey sum
national.summary: A postcard from Jack Phillips, the Titanic's chief radio officer, was postmarked April 6, 1912, four days before the ill-fated ship set sail.
national.body: A rare postcard from a Titanic crew member that features the famed ocean liner and was sent less than a week before its doomed voyage in 1912 sold at auction for over $41,000, according to a U.K. auction house.The postcard from Jack Phillips, the Titanic's chief radio officer, was postmarked April 6, 1912, four days before the ill-fated ship set sail on its maiden voyage across the Atlantic from Southampton, England, for New York City.Phillips, who turned 25 on the ship, sent the postcard to his sister, Elsie Phillips, according to auction house Henry Aldridge and Son Ltd."Thanks very much for your letter. Having glorious weather, went to Cowes yesterday. Will write later before we sail. Love all, Jack," Phillips wrote on the back of the postcard.The front features a picture of the Titanic at Southampton in southern England. The auction house said the postcard was in "very good to fine condition, with some light soiling and toning."According to the auction house, the postcard sold for 32,000 British pounds, or around $41,800. With taxes and fees, the final cost was 40,000 pounds, or around $52,300.During the trans-Atlantic crossing, on the night of April 14, 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg and eventually sank, killing over 1,500 people.As the Titanic was filling with water, Phillips stayed at his post and tried to get other ships to come to the rescue of the ocean liner's approximately 2,200 passengers and crew.According to the auction house, Phillips abandoned ship when the water reached his station, and he ultimately died from exposure to the severe cold on an overturned collapsible lifeboat.The ship's junior wireless officer, Harold Bride, hailed Phillips for his efforts, calling him "the man who saved us all," according to the auction house.Bride and Phillips, who also handled messages for passengers, received multiple iceberg warnings from other ships during the voyage and sent most of them along to the bridge. On the night the Titanic struck the iceberg, one warning about an ice field from another ship, the Mesaba, didn't make it to the bridge.

national.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. and arrives in Spain
national.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year, left the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.
national.body: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year and sent to a notorious prison in his home country, left the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, his team and the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid early Wednesday morning, alongside his wife, an American citizen, and his lawyer, a representative for the family told CBS News. national.title: Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
national.summary: Several Democratic senators have been signaling this move, saying the party needs to acknowledge the diverse class of incoming freshman that catapulted the party to victory in November.
national.body:
A group of Senate Democrats elected in 2024 sent a letter to colleagues Tuesday proposing to add an incoming freshman to the leadership ranks.

"These freshmen have their fingers on the pulse of long-time Democratic voters, those who voted for Democrats for the first time this past Election Day, and everyone in-between," the letter reads. "The deserve a seat at the table."

Senate Democrats have been signaling a desire to uplift new voices in the party.

"On election night, people voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership. That was very, very clear," Slotkin said during remarks at a conference of Democrats after the midterms .

New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker told MS NOW that leadership extends beyond the top post.

national.title: Images of asteroid targeted to test Earth's defences reveal stadium-sized crater
national.summary: The asteroid's surface was transformed after a spacecraft was deliberately crashed into it four years ago
national.body:
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.

Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.

"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.

"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."

The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).

It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.

national.title: Inflation remains stubbornly high, despite a drop in gas prices
national.summary: The Commerce Department said Wednesday that consumer prices rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September.
national.body:
Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — A key inflation gauge remained high last month even as gas price increases slowed in a sign that elevated costs remain a challenge for the Federal Reserve and elected officials in Washington.

The Commerce Department said Wednesday that consumer prices rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September. On a monthly basis, consumer prices climbed 0.3% from September to October, down from a 0.6% increase the previous month.

The stubbornly elevated price figures come as the economy is expanding at a healthy pace, driven by strong consumer spending and surging business investment as large tech firms splurge on building out AI infrastructure. Consumer spending has been resilient even as persistent inflation raises the costs of many necessities and has soured most Americans on the economy. Yet much of the spending is driven by upper-income households, and there are signs poorer Americans are relying more on credit to sustain their spending.

Gas prices rose just 0.8% last month, according to the department, after surging 9.2% in September. Food prices, however, jumped 0.4% from September to October, the biggest monthly increase since April.

Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core inflation accelerated to 3.3% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.1% in September. On a monthly basis, core prices rose 0.3% for the third month in a row.

The yearly core figure is now at its highest level in three years and above the Fed's target of 2%, which will likely intensify concerns among Fed officials that inflation is getting worse and further rate hikes are necessary.

Also Wednesday, the government said that the economy grew even faster in the July-September quarter than previously estimated, with growth revised upward to a 4.3% annual rate, the fastest in three years.

national.body:
Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

national.body:

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

The new tariffs proposed on Wednesday are meant to discourage excessive factory output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

The new tariffs stem from investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy.

"We've talked to our trading partners about this — they know what we're proposing," Greer told CNBC. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now."

The tariffs, rolled out the day before Thanksgiving, represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.

The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

The ship, known as "Griffin" or "Gribshunden," was the warship of Denmark's 15th-century leader King Hans. The ship was also used for diplomatic expeditions. In 1495, there was an explosion that led to the ship catching fire and sinking while anchored north of Sweden's Stora Ekö Island. The wreck was discovered in the 1970s. The latest discovery of the chain mail armor was made by team of experts from the United Kingdom's University of Southampton and Swedish institutions Södertörn University and Stockholm University, who have been conducting joint expeditions of the wreck since 2019. The chain mail armor is made of copper-alloy, the university said. It was found while documenting an ammunition-tool chest just below the ship's forecastle, which was an elevated fighting platform at the front of the vessel. Military gear may have been stored in the area, said Dr. Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, a visiting fellow at the University of Southampton's Centre for Maritime Archaeology, in the news release. German mercenaries, known as Landsknechts, were aboard the ship when it sank in 1495, Pacheco-Ruiz said. "It was truly an amazing find!" Pacheco-Ruiz said in the news release. national.title: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
national.summary: The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
national.body:
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.

In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.

Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.

The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".

In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".

"It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.

The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.

Political analyst Khanyi Magubane said the court ruling was a victory for Ramaphosa as it gave him "political and constitutional credibility".

A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.

Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.

"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.

Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.

"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."

In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.

"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.

Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.

"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.

Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.

Alexa St. John, Associated Press Alexa St. John, Associated Press

The U.S. Army detonated a dangerous and degraded stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday.

LIVE UPDATES: Army detonates stockpile of lead azide in Iowa

Here's what to know about lead azide, and why local officials and scientists have some concerns about potential health and environmental effects from the planned explosion.

Lead azide, which typically appears as a white or colorless crystalline powder or needlelike crystals, is a highly sensitive chemical compound containing lead and nitrogen.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The compound is used as an initiating explosive in munitions, and historically has been used in detonators to set off other explosives, such as TNT.

It is sensitive to shock, heat, impact and friction, and may explode when dry. With temperature changes and time, lead azide can form unstable, larger crystals that are even more sensitive.

The U.S. Army has detonated the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa after warning that the degrading bomb-making chemicals could otherwise explode at any time. The controlled detonation of roughly 5 tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown has set off concerns about potential health and environmental effects.

WATCH LIVE: Army expected to carry out controlled detonation of Iowa lead azide stockpile

Officials on Tuesday warned residents near Middletown to be ready to evacuate to avoid toxic dust in the air. The wind is expected to blow southwest — away from the nearby city of Burlington and the Mississippi River. The Army has also taken steps to limit the plume with barriers around the blast zone and ballistic gels to absorb the lead dust.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The blast was originally planned for last Friday, but the Army rescheduled to allow more time for extra safety measures and more favorable wind conditions, according to court documents. It was the third time the Army had changed the date, winning approval from a federal appeals court after environmentalists sued to stop the detonation.

The environmental groups that had sued in hopes of halting Wednesday's detonation said it was legal action and public pressure that prompted the Army to take more protective measures to limit the effects of the detonation.

"Iowa and neighboring states deserve a full accounting of why the situation was allowed to get to the point of crisis," said Sarah Green, executive director of the Iowa Environmental Council.

"I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it's absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley two hours after the blast.

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.

The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.

"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.

Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.

Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.

national.title: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
national.summary: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.
national.body:
Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving. Eddie Raynes hide caption

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

national.title: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
national.summary: 59% of U.S. shoppers plan to use AI for holiday shopping this weekend, according to the National Retail Federation
national.body:
This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation .

But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.

Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.

Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.

Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.

After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.

"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."

Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.

national.summary: Odochie rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
national.body:
Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.

In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.

The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.

national.title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
national.summary: Leaked data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia.
national.body:
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.

The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.

BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.

Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.

Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.

The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.

Iowans are hunkering down as the US Army prepares to blow up five tonnes of degraded explosives - with some fearing the controlled blast could be disastrous, even as others just want it done with.

The Army has argued a controlled detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly volatile compound used as a detonator, was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion.

The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the city of Middletown will go ahead at 09:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Wednesday, after an appeals court overturned a decision to stop the blast over concerns about potential lead exposure.

Officials have announced a five-mile (8km) optional evacuation zone and a 20-mile shelter-in-place advisory.

They estimate that airborne lead dust could travel 100 miles, depending on weather and wind.

Those who have chosen to stay have been told to remain indoors around the blast time and expect "temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead".

The urgency has increased because the US Army said it feared an uncontrolled explosion would become more likely as temperatures fell in the coming days.

Many people in the area are from families who have been there for generations - working in farming, manufacturing or at the ammunition plant itself.

local.title: Brighton preparing for first phase of its Multiversity Trail project
local.summary: The town is focusing on a stretch of the Lehigh Valley Trail that will be part of the network.
local.body:
The town of Brighton has received a $1.4 million grant from the state to improve a section of the Lehigh Valley Trail between the University of Rochester and Rochester Institute of Technology.

The work is part of the town's Multiversity Trail effort that aims to link the university, RIT, and Monroe Community College campuses using the Lehigh Valley Trail and the Erie Canalway Trail. On the Lehigh Valley Trail leg, the town plans to replace most of the surface, among other things.

"It's an old rail trail, the old Lehigh Valley train line, but you know it really needs upgrading, accessibility, signage, drainage issues," Brighton Supervisor Bill Moehle said. "So we'll be able to address all of those and more with this grant."

Moehle added that the town also wants to install flashing beacons at major road crossings that trail users would be able to activate, similar to the Auburn Trail.

Local News Brighton wants to connect bike trails for students at 3 campuses Jeremy Moule The town has three colleges within and along its borders. It wants students at them to be able to easily bike between campuses. The Lehigh Valley Trail work marks the first phase of the Multiversity Trail project. The town plans to put out a request for proposals around design work early next year.

Moehle said the project will benefit more than the college communities. The Lehigh trail is well used, he said, and an important connector for people living on the west side of town.

"It'll focus on the connection between the U of R and RIT because, you know, we have something there to work with," Moehle said. "There is an existing trail, and this will make it really much more user friendly for all users."

local.title: State announces increased road patrols during holiday weekend
local.summary: Motorists heading out for the holiday are being urged to play it safe. On Wednesday, state Gov. Kathy Hochul announced State Police and local law enforcement agencies statewide will increase patrols to target impaired and reckless driving during the Thanksgiving travel season. Funded by the Governor
local.body:
Motorists heading out for the holiday are being urged to play it safe.

On Wednesday, state Gov. Kathy Hochul announced State Police and local law enforcement agencies statewide will increase patrols to target impaired and reckless driving during the Thanksgiving travel season. Funded by the Governor's Traffic Safety Committee (GTSC), the impaired driving enforcement mobilization will run through Sunday.

"As we gather with friends and family to celebrate Thanksgiving, I want to ensure that everyone gets where they are going safely and not have what should be happy memories marred by a preventable tragedy," Hochul said. "I urge drivers to stay alert, stay sober and move over when you see vehicles stopped on the side of the road. If you're in a vehicle, you should wear seat belts or use proper restraint. I thank our law enforcement for sacrificing their time with loved ones to work on Thanksgiving and throughout the holidays to help keep New York's roadways safe."

In addition to increased traffic volume, the Thanksgiving holiday period is also associated with increased alcohol use. During the 2025 Thanksgiving holiday period, law enforcement officers arrested 2,236 drivers for driving while impaired by alcohol or drugs, 12,496 for speeding and also issued 3,075 tickets to unbelted drivers and passengers.

New York State Police Superintendent Steven G. James said, "Our members work vigilantly year-round to keep our roadways safe and prevent the needless tragedies that result from impaired and reckless driving. As always, we will be doing our part to ensure the holidays are safe for all who live in and travel through our great state. Please think twice before getting behind the wheel of a vehicle if you've been drinking. If you have had alcohol, there are several options available that will provide you with a safe ride to your destination. Together, let's make safety a top priority on our roadways this holiday season."

The State Police will supplement regular patrols statewide through efforts including fixed sobriety checkpoints and utilizing Concealed Identity Traffic Enforcement (CITE) patrol vehicles to better spot distracted drivers and those talking or texting on handheld devices. These unmarked vehicles blend in with everyday traffic but are unmistakable as emergency vehicles once the emergency lighting is activated.

Mtorists must follow the state's Move Over law, which was expanded in March 2024 to require drivers to slow down and move over for all vehicles stopped along the roadway if they can safely do so. The Thruway Authority and state Department of Transportation urge motorists to stay alert while driving, slow down and safely move over when they see a vehicle on the side of the road. The lives of motorists, employees, roadway workers and emergency personnel depend on it.

local.title: RIT researchers test 3D bioprinting as a possible key to unlock medical breakthroughs
local.summary: In the basement of the College of Art and Design, Professor Ahasan Habib picks up a flat, flexible, web-like printout that illustrates one step of many toward a dream to bio-print skin grafts, prosthetics and, one day, organs.
local.body:
Listen • 1:38 Rochester Institute of Technology researchers are working to create something like skin from scratch.

In the basement of the College of Art and Design, Professor Ahasan Habib picks up a flat, flexible, web-like printout that had been sitting in a drawer. It illustrates one step of many toward a dream to biologically print skin grafts, prosthetics and, one day, organs using a 3D printer.

"As an engineer, our goal is to make the technology that, like really, doctor, biomedical engineer, or biomedical professionals can use it for their purpose," Habib said.

Habib's vision is to use a type of material that is mostly comprised of water called hydrogel, infuse it with someone's stem cells, and then 3D print that concoction into tissue that would then become part of that person's body, with minimal risk of rejection — theoretically.

It's a vision shared by many in the interdisciplinary field of biotechnology. NASA astronauts have performed tests in microgravity in recent years, and researchers at the University of Miami’s Miller School of Medicine have an entire facility dedicated to 3D bioprinting.

In practice, there are logistical problems to solve before that could become reality. Such as: What exactly is the right combination of material to work with to account for the complexities of the human body?

"There's all sorts of parameters like even outside of like the very physical, like does it print well?" said Schuyler Mann, a dual-degree student in the engineering department. "Does it resist UV light? Can it support bacteria, if that's important for the application? How well can it sustain itself on its own?"

Mann is months away from graduation, and he works with Habib on bioprinting research for his capstone project.

local.title: Native Made Market brings Indigenous artisans, fashion and culture to downtown Rochester
local.summary: The fifth annual event will take over the Central Library downtown this weekend on Small Business Saturday, blending holiday shopping with cultural preservation.
local.body:
Rochester’s fifth annual Native Made Market will take over the Central Library downtown this weekend on Small Business Saturday, blending holiday shopping with cultural preservation.

The free gathering will feature Indigenous artisans, designers and educators from across Rochester, along with traditional dance, storytelling and fashion shows representing all six Haudenosaunee nations.

For Angelina Hilton, organizing Rochester’s Native Made Market is personal.

She’s an enrolled member of the Sac and Fox Nation, and she said fewer than 500 members remain in the Kansas-based tribe — a reality that adds urgency to bringing Native American culture into the wider community.

"It's important to preserve the fact that we were here and are still here, and are going to be here, because we're here to steward for at least the next seven generations," she said.

Hilton launched the market in 2022 inside her family’s cafe to counter what she saw as a lack of visibility for local Native people. Bringing a gathering to the Central Library carries its own significance, she said.

"We're telling our own stories in a place that shares stories with community, which hasn't historically, authentically represented Indigenous people and voices," Hilton said.

The market will be held from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday at Rochester’s Central Library on South Avenue. Admission is free.

local.body:
SANBORN -- Jodan Wright scored 21 points, grabbed seven rebounds and dished out six assists to lead the Jamestown Community College men's basketball team to an 84-79 victory over Mohawk Valley CC in the Niagara Tournament on Sunday.

The win, the Jayhawks' second of the weekend, improved their record to 4-2.

Julius Jeffries and Jasper Meissner added 19 points apiece for Coach Xavier Churnac's crew, who rallied from a 52-48 deficit at halftime.

Jordan Mason paced Mohawk Valley CC (4-4) with 28 points, Josh Harris had 15, and Micah-Jarrell Stewart and Micah Johnson chipped in 12 and 10, respectively.

Jamestown CC began the weekend with a 73-71 win Saturday over Genesee CC.

Wright turned in another dynamite performance, finishing with 27 points, nine boards, three assists and two blocks.

Meissner added 12 points for the Jayhawks, who trailed 39-30 at halftime, but outscored Genesee CC 43-32 after the break.

Leading the way for Genesee CC were Joshua Henry with 21 points and Luke Little with 19.

For hunting and fishing families across Western New York, Thanksgiving is about much more than turkey, stuffing and pumpkin pie. It’s a celebration of family, tradition, the outdoors, and the wonderful harvest that comes from the woods, waters and farms we are fortunate to call home.

Of course, a traditional Thanksgiving dinner wouldn’t be complete without the familiar favorites: a golden turkey, mashed potatoes and gravy, homemade stuffing, cranberry relish, squash, Brussels sprouts and a collection of pies that somehow always find room on an already crowded table. In many outdoor households, there’s also room for something a little more wild.

Venison, bear, pheasant, duck, wild turkey, rabbit and locally caught fish can all find their way onto our local holiday menu. These dishes bring something special to the celebration: a connection to the outdoors, memories of successful hunts and fishing trips, and the satisfaction of sharing food harvested by family and friends.

A few years ago, I had the pleasure of meeting Moira Tidball of Seneca County, a Cornell Cooperative Extension nutrition educator and the founder of the Wild Harvest Table. Launched in January 2009, the website celebrates the culinary bounty of wild game and fish throughout New York’s Finger Lakes region. It offers tested recipes, nutritional information and practical preparation techniques that make cooking wild harvests approachable and enjoyable.

Moira’s partner, Dr. Keith G. Tidball of Cornell University’s Department of Natural Resources and Environment, helped bring the project to life, recognizing its potential to explore the connections between hunting, fishing, food and community. Along with Dr. Paul Curtis of DNRE, the team secured USDA funding for research titled Leveraging the Locavore Movement: Exploring Family and Community Food Decision-making. The project examined how locally harvested foods influence the ways families procure, prepare and enjoy their meals. The effort also helped bring nutritional information for several wild species into USDA FoodData Central.

The result is a terrific resource for anyone looking to bring a little more wild harvest to the dinner table. From venison and bear to squirrel, grouse, pheasant, waterfowl, wild turkey, walleye, trout and bass, there’s plenty of inspiration to be found at www.wildharvesttable.com. I’ve tried the recipes myself, and they’re delicious without requiring a culinary degree or an entire afternoon of kitchen negotiations.

local.title: Trustees seek direct Dunkirk water link
local.summary: Fredonia’s incessant water supply debate saw another bend in its stream Monday. Two trustees are suggesting a halt on plans to connect with the North County Water District through the town of Pomfret’s infrastructure. Trustees Tim Mulholland and LeeAnn Lazarony want Fredonia to instead revisit a pla
local.body:
Fredonia's incessant water supply debate saw another bend in its stream Monday. Two trustees are suggesting a halt on plans to connect with the North County Water District through the town of Pomfret's infrastructure.

Trustees Tim Mulholland and LeeAnn Lazarony want Fredonia to instead revisit a plan for connecting directly with the city of Dunkirk.

"This was actually something that was looked at," Mulholland noted at a Board of Trustees meeting. He did most of the talking about the proposal; Lazarony was attending remotely and had occasional microphone issues.

Indeed, a previous edition of Fredonia's Board of Trustees approved a plan to connect directly with Dunkirk in December 2023. However, a group of village residents successfully sued to halt that plan. No one mentioned that lawsuit at Tuesday's meeting.

Fredonia later pivoted to its current plan to connect with the NCWD through Pomfret -- though it recently suspended engineering on the project due to funding issues. Dunkirk's water plant also supplies the NCWD in addition to the city's own direct customers.

"The fact that the interconnection worked really triggered this thought process again for us," Mulholland said. The village acquired more than 900,000 gallons from Dunkirk, through an existing line that connects with a pump station on Vineyard Drive, in October during boil water and conservation orders. However, that line does not have sufficient capacity to supply all of Fredonia's water needs.

Mulholland stated NCWD "engineers have identified several steps in their preliminary plans making (the current connection plan) a complicated proposal." He noted that pressure reducing valves, new mains and a new storage tank would be required.

That would drive the project costs over $21.5 million, he said. But estimated costs of connecting directly with Dunkirk in 2023 were only around $5 million, he said.

According to the state’s measles dashboard website, that number had not increased as of Tuesday morni
local.body:
It was announced at the Chautauqua County Board of Health meeting Thursday that there have been 10 cases of measles reported in the county. According to the state's measles dashboard website, that number had not increased as of Tuesday morning.

Lacey Wilson, Chautauqua County public health director, said due to privacy laws, the state won't report the outbreak by zip codes.

"There's so few numbers, they could easily be identifiable," she said.

Wilson declined to say if any of those individuals have been hospitalized. She did add that there have been no deaths due to measles in Chautauqua County as of the time of the interview.

For those who suspect they may have measles, Wilson asked people to call their doctor first instead of going directly to the emergency room.

"What we're concerned about is exposure to other people, so call a health care provider and seek their guidance as to what your next steps should be," she said.

On Sept. 2 health officials announced the first case of measles of measles in Chautauqua County in more than 30 years.

For neighboring New York counties, Erie County has two cases, while Cattaraugus County has five confirmed cases.

local.title: New book tells the story of the Onondaga Nation
local.summary: Author and scholar Michael Leroy Oberg has done extensive research on the story of the Onondaga Nation. He joins "Connections with Evan Dawson" on Nov. 25, 2026 to share what he thinks we all should know.
local.body:
Listen • 52:08 1 of 2 — Image (59).jpg Michael Oberg with host Evan Dawson on "Connections with Evan Dawson" on Wednesday, November 25, 2026 George Yeadon / WXXI News 2 of 2 — book-cover.png How much do you know about the Iroquois?

Author and scholar Michael Leroy Oberg brings the struggles and the resilience of the Onondaga Nation to life in his book, “The Central Fire of the Iroquois: A Five-Hundred-Year History of the Onondaga Nation.”

Oberg writes of the many threats and attacks on the Indigenous population. The story involves a rise, a fall, and a rise into the modern era, along with the hope of self-determination.

For those who feel like they don’t fully understand the story of the Onondaga Nation — or who were taught only caricatures — these lessons will be new and vital.

Every month, Billboard Latin and Billboard Español editors spotlight a group of rising artists whose music we love. Why They Should Be on Your Radar: Earlier this year, Colombian artist Pipe Bueno teamed up with Cumbia Pedregal on “Dime Que Me Hiciste” — a winning blend of smooth, irresistibly-catchy cumbia with a distinct sound. Made up of brothers Emilio, José Pablo, and Luche Zepeda, this trio feels like a band of old souls reincarnated in 2026 with influences from pop, banda grupera, and regional Mexican music, among others. The more I listened to their music, the more I discovered elements of 1980s Latin America: long hair, colorful suits, and soft vocals that seem to sigh through the verses.

Grupo Pedregal’s musical and visual style stands out amid today’s hard-hitting, rhythmic sounds — embracing love songs, heartbreak and clean lyrics rooted in the timeless spirit of Mexican music. In May, the group released its debut album, Sabor a Llanto , featuring “Mi Peor Apuesta,” its second collaboration with singer-songwriter Eden Muñoz (following 2025’s “Sin Ti No Sé Vivir”). — INGRID FAJARDO

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: When I first discovered Cuba’s reparto music, one of the first artists that captured by attention, mainly because of his lyrical content, was El Dukesito. With songs such as “La Oportunidad” and “Voy A Mi” — songs that are rooted in personal growth and potent affirmations, rather than the common provocative and street slang that characterizes the genre — I knew he was a special breed.

Born Nassir Cristo Duquesne Dublón in La Habana, the Miami-based artist dubs himself as “el más completo y versátil de la nueva” (the most complete and versatile artist of the new generation) — and his “No Llores Por El,” a ranchera-tinged pop song released this year with Bambino the Boss attests to that. With his crystalline vocals, the 30-year-old artist, who’s signed to Rami Récords, has received the stamp of approval from Cuban pioneers including Gente de Zona, Chocolate MC, and Wow Popy. Dukesito is currently making the rounds with his new singles “Solo Solito” and “Tu No Sientes” with Yeyo Pa’ Que Sepa — both released under Plus Media. — JESSICA ROIZ

entertainment.title: Sarah Michelle Gellar Reveals Her, Freddie Prinze Jr.'s Holiday Plans
entertainment.summary: Sarah Michelle Gellar knows the best way to slay the holiday season. And for the Buffy the Vampire Slayer and husband Freddie Prinze Jr., it all comes down to focusing on their community—a...
entertainment.body:
Sarah Michelle Gellar knows the best way to slay the holiday season.

And for the Buffy the Vampire Slayer and husband Freddie Prinze Jr. , it all comes down to focusing on their community—a tradition that dates back to her own childhood.

“A lot of times for Christmas and New Year's, we're traveling, so Thanksgiving is something that's always been important to be at home for,” Gellar told E! News in an exclusive interview. “When I was younger my mom always used to open our apartment to anyone that couldn't afford to go home or didn't have family. So, we do the same. We're actually having probably one of the largest Thanksgivings we've had in a couple years this year.”

That said, there is plenty of quiet family time amid the busy day with guests. And it’s those traditions with kids Charlotte , 17, and Rocky , 14, that have stood the test of time. In fact, Gellar admitted that when it comes to their family holiday traditions, “what's funny is they haven't really evolved” as the kids have gotten older.

“I grew up in New York City, so Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is obviously very important,” Gellar noted. “I used to go the night before and watch them blow up all the floats—you'd sit there and you'd bring your thermos of hot chocolate because it'd be freezing, and you'd watch. And so I've grown up with that parade, and I, from the time my kids were born, I'm like, we will be watching this parade."

In fact, a pre-Thanksgiving work trip to New York City was enough to have her eldest wondering if their favorite tradition might be put on pause. “When my daughter was knew I was leaving, she's like, ‘You're going to be back for the parade, right?’” Gellar revealed. “I'm like, ‘The parade's on Thanksgiving. I will be home. You don't have to worry.’ So, the Thanksgiving Day grade is always like a really big a big one for us.”

Plus, there’s the sprint to get the decorations up—and wind down with a movie marathon. On the docket this year is Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping and checking out Ariana Grande in Focker-in-Law.

“Getting a tree up is always that weekend,” she explained. “Also for us going to the movies like that weekend because it's always a great movie weekend. So we've already got our tickets. We got our tickets for to see Hunger Games . We have our tickets ready to go to see Ariana in Fockers . We're ready to go."

entertainment.title: Luke Bryan & Luke Combs Channel Old-School Influences in ‘Finders Keepers’: ‘I Want to Put Songs Out That Could Go Right Into The Set List’
entertainment.summary: Billboard's Makin' Tracks column looks at the writing and recording behind the Luke Bryan and Luke Combs collaboration "Finders Keepers."
entertainment.body:
“Luke-ing” back across the years, Luke Bryan didn’t have much country competition in branding his name.

Hank Williams recorded a series of recitations under the pseudonym Luke the Drifter, and stretching the boundaries a bit, Waylon Jennings had a landmark hit with “Luckenbach, Texas (Back to the Basics of Love).” Bryan got used to being known in the genre by a single syllable until a “Hurricane” hit in 2016.

“I thought I had the Luke name,” Bryan says. “I thought I had that solidly before Luke Combs. I mean, the disc jockeys could just say, ‘That was Luke.’ They didn’t have to verify last names.” Related Dolly Parton to Receive CNN Heroes Legacy Award, Miley Cyrus to Accept on Her Behalf ESSENCE Festival of Culture Moving On From New Orleans After Three Decades: 'Memories Were Made -- And So Was History' Noah Kahan Caps Epic Year With 'Live From the Great Divide' Album Explore Luke Bryan Luke Combs See latest videos, charts and news

Not that Bryan has a problem with the situation. In fact, he enlisted Combs as a feature voice on “Finders Keepers,” released by Row Crop/MCA Nashville to country radio via PlayMPE on Oct. 12. It lists on Billboard’s Country Airplay as “Luke Bryan & Luke Combs,” though Bryan doesn’t particularly care how people refer to them.

The song’s writers were just happy they got the call. Bryan heard it — and recorded it — 15 days after its official date of creation when his manager, KP Entertainment founder/president Kerri Edwards, was going through unopened emails during Bryan’s session at Nashville’s Ocean Way on March 6. She played it for Bryan and his producers, Jeff and Jody Stevens, during their drive to Dicey’s Tavern on a lunch break, and they added it to that afternoon’s material. The musicians picked it up easily.

“They ran through it one time, and ran through it another time, and that was it,” Jeff recalls.

Songwriter Sam Ellis (“What If I Never Get Over You,” “More Hearts Than Mine”) hosted the writing session that spawned “Finders Keepers” on Feb. 19 at his East Nashville studio. When the initial song ideas fell flat for Ellis and his co-writers, Jimi Bell (“Backup Plan,” “Last Night Lonely”) and Beau Bailey (“Stay Country or Die Tryin’,” “Favorite Country Song”), Bailey apologetically mentioned a hook he’d concocted during a brainstorming exercise: “Finders keepers, losers drinkers.” No apology was necessary; his co-writers loved the wordplay.

entertainment.title: New Doc Reveals How Andrew Tate’s ‘False Braggadocio’ Is Just Like His Dad’s: ‘It’s Spooky’
entertainment.summary: Andrew Tate: Toxic Empire uses interview with former friends, associates, and even acquaintances of his father to chart the manosphere influencer's rise to fame
entertainment.body:
British-American brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate are currently awaiting extradition to the U.K., where they face dozens of charges including rape and trafficking for the purpose of sexual exploitation. The photos they posted on social media as they rose to fame — of men in tight pants, gripping thick cigars in their teeth, leaning against luxury sports cars next to big-breasted women in bikinis — helped to establish the manosphere, and have become tropes in their own right. Their exploits — running a cam-girl empire out of Romania, which allegedly engaged in human trafficking — have been widely documented, as have their denials that they engaged in any kind of illegal activity.

But how did they really make that money, and who are the survivors they’ve left in their wake? The new documentary, Andrew Tate : Toxic Empire , attempts to answer those questions, using interviews with former members of their exclusive networking group, the War Room; with women who allege they were sexually assaulted by the brothers, including the former anti-feminist provocateur Lauren Southern; and those who knew them in their younger days, including Andrew’s fellow Big Brother castmember, who was there during his brief run on the British reality show back in 2016. (Like everything else, the brothers deny the allegations of sexual assault.)

Though many have tried to make sense of their story, Toxic Empire lays it out in stark relief: their childhood in the council flats of Luton, England, far away from their chess-master father back in the states; their short-lived stints as kickboxers; their entry into the cam-girl management business, long before OnlyFans made online sex work mainstream; and their brotherly dynamic, with Andrew, 39, taking the front seat, while his younger brother, 38, played support.

The first two parts of the four-part docuseries premieres on Nov. 25 at 9 p.m. on ID; the next two episodes will come out over the following two weeks, and all of them will be available on HBO Max after they air. Here’s three things we learned from the first two episodes.
